filesystem-and-navigation.r: A team shipped a new release by pointing a symbolic link called current at a fresh release folder. The rollback was supposed to be one command, but a cleanup job had already deleted the old folder, so the link pointed at nothing and the service stayed down until the files were restored from backup. Keep the last two releases and test the link before you delete anything.
filesystem-and-navigation.x: Treat the filesystem layout as an interface. Decide which paths are state and which are disposable, mount state separately, make releases immutable and switch them with an atomic link change. In review, ask what happens to the previous release and who is allowed to delete it.

users-groups-permissions.r: A deployment worked on every server except one, where the application could not read its config file. The file was owned by root with mode 600 on that host only, because someone had edited it by hand with sudo. The fix took two minutes once the owner and mode were compared, and the real fix was to set them in configuration management.
users-groups-permissions.x: Permissions are a policy, so aim for the smallest set that works: one service account per service, group-based access for humans, no shared logins and no world-writable paths. Review sudo rules and setuid files on a schedule, and prefer capabilities over running as root.

processes-and-services.r: A service kept dying overnight and nobody noticed until morning. The unit file had no restart policy, so a single crash left it stopped. Adding Restart=on-failure with a short delay and a start limit kept it up, and the journal showed the crash was a memory limit that needed raising.
processes-and-services.x: A unit file is operational design. Choose restart policy, start limits, resource limits, ordering and a clean stop signal on purpose, and make sure a restart loop is visible instead of silent. Ask what the service does on SIGTERM and how long it needs to drain.

disks-and-filesystems.r: Alerts said a disk was full, yet the files added up to far less than the disk size. A deleted log file was still held open by a running process, so the space was never freed. Restarting the process released it, and a proper log rotation with a reopen signal prevented a repeat.
disks-and-filesystems.x: Capacity is more than bytes: inodes, reserved blocks, open-but-deleted files and snapshots all count. Alert on growth rate and time to full, not just a percentage, and put logs and data on separate filesystems so one cannot starve the other.

lvm-and-raid.r: A database volume ran short of space during a busy week. Because it sat on LVM with free space in the volume group, the team grew the volume and the filesystem while the database stayed online. A week later a disk failed in the mirror, and RAID kept serving while the spare rebuilt.
lvm-and-raid.x: RAID protects against a disk failing, not against deletion, corruption or a bad write, so it never replaces backups. Plan rebuild time and the risk of a second failure during it, monitor array health, and test a restore before you need one.

package-management.r: A routine update on one server pulled a newer library version than the rest of the fleet, and a service that depended on the old behavior started failing. Pinning the package version and mirroring the repository internally meant every host got the same bytes on the same day.
package-management.x: Treat packages as supply chain. Pin versions, use an internal mirror, verify signatures, roll updates in stages with a canary and keep the ability to roll back. Ask how fast you could patch a critical vulnerability across the whole fleet.

ssh-and-remote-access.r: An engineer left the company and their key stayed in authorized_keys on dozens of servers for months. A routine audit found it. The team moved to short-lived certificates issued by a central authority, so access expired by itself and removing someone took one change.
ssh-and-remote-access.x: Aim for no long-lived keys on servers: certificates with short lifetimes, a bastion or session manager with logging, agent forwarding off by default and root login disabled. The question to ask is how you would revoke one person's access in minutes.

cron-and-timers.r: A nightly backup script ran perfectly when tested by hand but did nothing under cron. The job had a different PATH and no home directory variables, so the command it called was not found, and the error went to a mailbox nobody read. Using absolute paths and sending output to the log fixed it.
cron-and-timers.x: Scheduled jobs fail silently unless you design for it: lock against overlap, set timeouts, log start and finish, alert on a missing run rather than only on an error, and think about what happens when the host was off at the scheduled time.

logs-and-troubleshooting.r: Customers reported random failures between 02:10 and 02:20. Lining up the application log, the kernel log and the journal by timestamp showed the kernel killed a process for using too much memory exactly at 02:12. The log lines were each harmless alone; together they told the story.
logs-and-troubleshooting.x: Logs help only if they are complete, timestamped consistently and searchable when the host is gone. Ship them off the box, standardise formats and time zones, and set retention by what you need to investigate, not by disk size.

performance-triage.r: A server felt slow and the first guess was CPU. Load average was high, but vmstat showed processes waiting on disk and iostat showed the disk at its limit, so adding CPUs would have changed nothing. Moving a noisy backup job to a quiet hour cleared the problem.
performance-triage.x: Use a method, not hunches: check utilisation, saturation and errors for CPU, memory, disk and network in a fixed order. Beware of averages that hide spikes, and remember that a problem seen on the host may be caused by a neighbour or a dependency.

boot-and-kernel.r: After a kernel update a server did not come back from a reboot. Someone reached the console, chose the previous kernel from the boot menu and the machine started normally. The team then kept two kernels installed and tested reboots in staging before production.
boot-and-kernel.x: Reboots are risky events. Keep a known-good kernel, have out-of-band console access, test the boot path after changes to disks and init settings, and know how to reach rescue mode before you are in a hurry.

security-hardening.r: A scan flagged a server running a database port open to the whole internet because a default firewall rule was never removed. Nothing had been stolen yet, but the exposure had lasted months. A default-deny firewall and a short list of allowed sources closed it.
security-hardening.x: Hardening is about reducing surface and limiting the damage of a compromise: minimal packages, default-deny network rules, least privilege, mandatory access control kept on, patching and audit logs shipped off the host. Ask what an attacker gets after the first foothold.

namespaces-and-cgroups.r: A container kept being killed even though the host had plenty of free memory. The container had a cgroup memory limit that was lower than the application needed, so the kernel killed it when it crossed that line. Raising the limit and fixing a leak stopped the restarts.
namespaces-and-cgroups.x: A container is a process with namespaces and cgroup limits, not a small virtual machine, so it shares the kernel and its weaknesses. Understand which limits apply, what is not isolated and why a kernel bug affects every container on the host.

working-efficiently-in-the-terminal.r: An engineer ran a destructive command in the wrong terminal window because two production and staging sessions looked identical. After that the team added the environment name to the prompt in a bright colour and used tmux session names, which made the mistake much harder to repeat.
working-efficiently-in-the-terminal.x: Efficiency and safety go together. Make the environment obvious in the prompt, use history search, aliases for dry runs and sessions that survive a dropped connection, and slow down for any command that cannot be undone.

time-ntp-and-timezones.r: A set of servers started rejecting logins because their clocks had drifted several minutes, which broke time-limited tokens. Fixing NTP on one host was easy, but the real lesson was to alert on clock offset and keep every server on UTC.
time-ntp-and-timezones.x: Time is a dependency of security, databases, certificates and distributed ordering. Monitor offset, use more than one time source, store and log in UTC, and be careful with leap seconds and virtual machine pauses.

systemd-overrides-targets-and-dependenci.r: Someone edited a vendor unit file directly to add an environment variable, and the next package update overwrote it and broke the service. A drop-in override file survived updates and was easy to review in version control.
systemd-overrides-targets-and-dependenci.x: Never edit vendor units; use drop-ins and keep them in configuration management. Understand the difference between ordering and requirement, and test what happens when a dependency fails, restarts or starts late.

kernel-modules-sysctl-and-boot-parameter.r: A busy server ran out of connection tracking entries during a traffic spike and started dropping packets. Raising the limit with sysctl fixed it right away, but the change was lost at the next reboot until it was saved in a file under /etc/sysctl.d.
kernel-modules-sysctl-and-boot-parameter.x: Kernel settings are production configuration. Change one at a time, record the reason, persist them in code, test under load and know the default so you can go back. Be cautious with settings copied from the internet.

processes-memory-and-the-oom-killer.r: A web server was killed by the out-of-memory killer even though the monitoring graph showed free memory. Most of the memory was page cache, which is reclaimable, but a sudden spike in a worker process had used the rest. Setting a memory limit per worker made failures local and predictable.
processes-memory-and-the-oom-killer.x: Read memory as available, not free, and understand overcommit, swap behaviour and cgroup limits. Decide which process should die first, set limits and memory-based alerts, and prefer a controlled restart to a random kill.

system-calls-strace-and-perf.r: A program hung at startup with no log output. Running it under strace showed it blocked trying to connect to an address that no longer existed, which explained everything in a minute. Without the trace the team had been guessing for hours.
system-calls-strace-and-perf.x: Tracing tools are powerful but have a cost: strace can slow a process a lot and should be used carefully in production. Know when to prefer sampling with perf or eBPF, and always compare a trace against a baseline.

filesystems-page-cache-and-io.r: A service wrote data and reported success, then the host lost power and some of the data was missing. The writes had reached the page cache but not the disk because the code never called fsync. Calling fsync at the right points, and accepting the speed cost, made the data durable.
filesystems-page-cache-and-io.x: Durability is a decision with a price. Know what your application, filesystem, controller cache and disk actually guarantee, and test with power loss or kill scenarios instead of assuming. Watch writeback stalls under heavy load.

networking-in-the-kernel-sockets-and-con.r: Clients saw intermittent connection timeouts under load even though the server CPU was low. The accept queue of the listening socket was full because the application accepted connections too slowly, so the kernel dropped new ones. A larger backlog and a faster accept loop removed the drops.
networking-in-the-kernel-sockets-and-con.x: Most mysterious network problems live in queues, state tables and timeouts: listen backlog, conntrack, ephemeral ports and TIME_WAIT. Measure queue depth and drops, and size limits from expected peak, not from average traffic.

debugging-a-sick-server.r: On a bad night an on-call engineer followed a fixed order: CPU, memory, disk, network, logs. Within ten minutes they found a full filesystem caused by a runaway debug log, cleared it, restarted the service and wrote a ticket for log limits. The checklist kept them calm when guessing would not have.
debugging-a-sick-server.x: A good checklist is a thinking aid, not a script. Stabilise first, collect evidence before restarting so the cause is not lost, change one thing at a time, and write down what you saw. Afterwards, turn each manual check into an alert or a runbook step.
